questions.q: What are the three repeating steps that make up an agent loop?
options: Plan, act, observe — then plan again using everything learned so far
Train, validate, deploy
Request, cache, retry
Prompt, fine-tune, evaluate
questions.explain: The model decides an action (plan), the action runs (act), and the result comes back into context (observe) — then the cycle repeats.

questions.q: In the Claude API, what signals that the model is done calling tools and ready to give its final answer?
options: The tools array is deleted from the request
A stop_reason of tool_use on every single response
The context window reaching its maximum size
A stop_reason of end_turn instead of tool_use
questions.explain: stop_reason: tool_use means the model wants to call a tool; stop_reason: end_turn means it's finished and is giving its final reply.

questions.q: Besides the model deciding it's done, what two other things can end an agent loop, per this lesson?
options: Deleting the system prompt, or restarting the server
A hard limit enforced by your code (step cap, budget, timeout), or a human intervening at a checkpoint
Switching to a different programming language, or disabling logging
Nothing else can end a loop — only the model can decide to stop
questions.explain: A production agent needs explicit limits and human checkpoints as backstops, because a model that never decides it's done would otherwise run forever.

questions.q: In the weather/support-tickets trace example, why couldn't the agent call get_weather on the very first iteration?
options: It didn't yet know which city to pass in — that came from the first tool's result
The agent is never allowed to call more than one tool total
get_weather doesn't require any arguments
get_weather must always be called before any other tool
questions.explain: The second call depended on the first call's observed result (the city), which is exactly why this requires a loop rather than one upfront plan.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue the loop can't be replaced by 'one planning step followed by several parallel actions'?
options: Because parallel actions are always slower than sequential ones
Because tools are not allowed to run in the same request
Because later steps in the trace depend on the real results of earlier steps, which aren't known until those earlier steps actually run
Because the model can only ever call one tool in its entire lifetime
questions.explain: You can't plan the get_weather call's arguments before you know the city, and you only learn the city by actually running and observing the first tool call.
